# ggumap

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/jeroenjanssens/ggumap/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/jeroenjanssens/ggumap/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/jeroenjanssens/ggumap/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/jeroenjanssens/ggumap)
[![extendr](https://img.shields.io/badge/extendr-*-276DC2)](https://extendr.rs/extendr/extendr_api/)
<!-- badges: end -->

ggumap adds UMAP to ggplot2. `geom_umap()` and `stat_umap()` compute a
[UMAP](https://umap-learn.readthedocs.io/) embedding of the layer data and
draw it, in a single step:

```{r example, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggumap)

ggplot(palmerpenguins::penguins, aes(colour = species)) +
  geom_umap(features = bill_length_mm:body_mass_g, scale = TRUE, na.rm = TRUE) +
  theme_umap()
```

* **Tidy feature selection.** Choose the input columns with `features`, using
  `dplyr::select()` syntax. All numeric columns are used by default.
* **Points, text, labels.** `geom_umap()` draws points, and
  `stat_umap(geom = "text")` or `"label"` annotate them. Aesthetics are carried
  along row by row and never split the embedding.
* **Fast.** The computation is done by Apple's multi-threaded Rust port of
  umap-learn and PyNNDescent, from
  [embedding-atlas](https://github.com/apple/embedding-atlas).
* **Stable plots.** Seeds are derived from the data, and results are cached:
  re-drawing, resizing or saving a plot does not move the points or recompute
  the embedding, and several layers share one embedding.
* **Facets.** One embedding for the whole layer (default) or one per panel.
* **Interruptible**, with a progress bar for long computations.

## Installation

ggumap needs a Rust toolchain (rustc >= 1.90) to build from source; see
<https://rust-lang.org/tools/install/>.

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("jeroenjanssens/ggumap")
```

## Usage

```{r layers, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
cars <- transform(mtcars, model = rownames(mtcars))

ggplot(cars, aes(label = model, colour = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_umap(scale = TRUE, n_neighbors = 5) +
  stat_umap(geom = "text", scale = TRUE, n_neighbors = 5,
            size = 2.5, vjust = -0.8, show.legend = FALSE,
            check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.15)) +
  labs(colour = "cylinders") +
  theme_umap()
```

`umap_embed()` gives you the embedding as a data frame, outside of a plot:

```{r embed}
umap_embed(iris, Sepal.Length:Petal.Width, seed = 1) |> head()
```

See `vignette("ggumap")` for more.

## Performance

ggumap is much faster than the [umap](https://cran.r-project.org/package=umap)
package, and on par with [uwot](https://cran.r-project.org/package=uwot):

<img src="man/figures/README-benchmark.png" alt="Line chart of the time to compute a UMAP embedding with ggumap, uwot and umap, for 1,000 to 20,000 observations." width="100%" />

```{r benchmark-table, echo = FALSE}
res <- read.csv("bench/results/readme.csv")
res <- res[res$n == max(res$n), ]
res$implementation <- ifelse(
  res$contender == "umap-naive",
  "umap (pure R)",
  paste0(sub("-0.5", "", res$contender), ", ", res$threads, ifelse(res$threads == 1, " thread", " threads"))
)
tab <- aggregate(cbind(seconds, trustworthiness) ~ implementation, res, stats::median)
tab <- tab[order(tab$seconds), ]
knitr::kable(
  tab,
  row.names = FALSE,
  digits = c(0, 1, 3),
  col.names = c("Implementation", "Seconds", "Trustworthiness"),
  caption = sprintf("%s observations, median of %d runs.", format(max(res$n), big.mark = ","), max(res$rep))
)
```

All three find embeddings of the same quality (trustworthiness measures how
well the embedding preserves the nearest neighbours of the input). With one
thread, uwot is somewhat faster than ggumap's default `flavour = "0.5"`; the
`flavour = "0.6"` pipeline was two to three times as fast as the default at
10,000 observations. See [`bench/`](https://github.com/jeroenjanssens/ggumap/tree/main/bench) for the methodology, and run
`just bench-readme` to reproduce the figure on your machine.
